items.title: Milt Hinton interviewed by Joe Williams, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995
items.q: like I came in Cab Calloway’s band with all these giants, Ben Webster, and Cab, and Doc Cheatham

ctx.x: Well I feel sorry, and that’s the reason I think so wonderful of you, and I see you out working and that’s what I do a great deal of, is trying to go around to the schools now, and impart some knowledge to these young people because they don’t have an

apprenticeship, for them to come in like we came in, like I came in Cab Calloway’s band with all these giants, Ben Webster, and Cab, and Doc Cheatham, you know, and I got a chance to learn something about discipline and things like that. We don’t have those bands for our young musicians, as with the masters, to sit down and watch them.

items.title: Hinton Milt — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Well later Mouse Randolph, Irving Randolph was… trumpet, and Doc Cheetum.

ctx.x: Who else was in the trumpet section, do you remember?

Well later Mouse Randolph, Irving Randolph was… trumpet, and Doc Cheetum. he came in there, not too… he came in there. Because Doc stayed… let‟s see it was Lemar Wright, Irving Randolph, and Doc Cheetum. Then we added… there was three trumpets at first when I came in about that time. Then they added a fourth trumpet and I think it was Chet Collins. Then Doc Cheetum got sick and went home to recuperate and someone recommended Dizzy and Dizzy came in and Doc never came back until years later in his „70s or…
Were you in the band when Dizzy was in the band?

items.title: Doc Cheatham interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, New York City, New York, July 28, 1995
items.q: was the subject of a recent Nightline interview with fellow jazz veterans Milt Hinton and Lionel Hampton

ctx.x: Doc Cheatham’s remarkable career in jazz reads like a fairy tale. Born Aldolphus Cheatham in 1905, he grew up in Nashville and took up the sax and trumpet at an early age. His first playing experience was at the Bijou Theater where he played behind Bessie Smith, later recording on the soprano sax with another blues great, Ma Rainey. His search for further playing opportunities took him to Chicago where he came under the spell of Louis Armstrong, eventually playing beside him and substituting when Satchmo was…
